subsection: 2. O'Neill and the Civil Rights movement, 1963–1969

notes.b: Terence O'Neill came to power in 1963 with a programme of economic modernisation and gestures towards Catholics and the Republic.
points: Terence O'Neill succeeded Brookeborough as Prime Minister in 1963, having been Minister of Finance in the previous government.
He promoted economic planning, drawing on the Matthew Report (1964) on regional planning and the Wilson Plan (1965) for economic development.
He made symbolic visits to Catholic schools and hospitals, which unionist hardliners resented as concessions.
In January 1965 he received the Taoiseach, Seán Lemass, at Stormont, a meeting widely described as the first of its kind since partition.
O'Neill returned the visit to Dublin later in 1965, and his policy of building bridges with the Republic became known as the 'bridge-building' approach.
The Stormont government's new universities and industrial estates were part of a wider plan to show that Northern Ireland could be modern and prosperous.
Catholics welcomed the gestures but judged that real change in housing, jobs and voting was too slow.

notes.b: O'Neill's reforms split his own party, and hardline unionists saw the Lemass meeting as the first step towards a united Ireland.
points: Ian Paisley founded the Free Presbyterian Church in 1951, and by the mid-1960s he was the leading Protestant critic of O'Neill's policies.
Paisley and other hardliners opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that it undermined the Union and Protestant identity.
William Craig, Minister of Home Affairs, was a hardline critic within the government and banned the Derry march of 5 October 1968.
Unionist MPs in the Stormont parliament and in the party organisation argued that O'Neill was giving away too much to nationalists.
The 'O'Neill must go' campaign, led by Paisley and others, sought the Prime Minister's removal from office.
O'Neill's position weakened as unionist opposition grew and as violence on both sides increased in 1968 and 1969.

notes.b: O'Neill was the reforming Prime Minister whose policies drove the civil rights movement and whose authority collapsed under its pressure.
points: He was born in 1914 into an aristocratic family in County Antrim and became Prime Minister in 1963 after a career in the Stormont cabinet.
He held the post of Minister of Finance from 1956 to 1963, where he developed the economic planning that later shaped his premiership.
He made modernisation and reconciliation the centre of his programme, and he tried to build contact with Catholics and with Dublin.
He participated directly in the events of 1968 and 1969, meeting civil rights leaders and making the five-point reform programme.
He announced his five-point reform package in late 1968 and explained his policy in the 'Ulster at the Crossroads' broadcast in December 1968.
He resigned as Prime Minister in April 1969 after a crisis in his party and a series of violent events in Derry and Belfast.
He was made a life peer in 1970 as Baron O'Neill of the Maine.
Contemporaries were divided: unionist hardliners branded him a traitor, while nationalists welcomed the gestures but judged them too slow.
Historians generally judge him a genuine reformer whose programme was real but late, and whose authority was constrained by his own party.

notes.h: Key personality: Conn and Patricia McCluskey
notes.b: The McCluskeys founded the Campaign for Social Justice, which turned evidence of discrimination in Dungannon into a national campaign.
points: Conn and Patricia McCluskey founded the Campaign for Social Justice in Northern Ireland in 1964 in Dungannon, County Tyrone.
The campaign gathered evidence on discrimination in housing allocation and local jobs, especially by the Dungannon district council.
It published its findings and made appeals to British MPs and the media, which brought the issue of discrimination to a wider audience.
The McCluskeys were participants in the campaign, and their work provided models and evidence for the civil rights movement that followed.
Some unionists dismissed the campaign as a front for republicans, a charge the campaign rejected.
Historians credit the Campaign for Social Justice with turning discrimination into a public issue before the Civil Rights Association was formed.

notes.h: The Civil Rights Association and its demands
notes.b: The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association was founded in 1967 to campaign for equal rights for Catholics on the British model.
points: NICRA was founded in 1967 and drew together nationalists, socialists, trade unionists and some liberal Protestants.
Its demands included one man, one vote in local elections, an end to gerrymandering, and fair allocation of council houses on a points system.
It also demanded the repeal of the Special Powers Act and the disbanding of the B Specials.
Its first march was from Coalisland to Dungannon on 24 August 1968, and it was followed by marches in Derry, Newry and Belfast.
The movement used peaceful marches and sit-ins to draw attention to discrimination, and it sought British support for reform.
The Stormont authorities banned or obstructed many marches, which led to confrontations with the police and loyalist counter-demonstrators.

notes.b: The banned civil rights march in Derry was broken up by police, and the footage shown on television turned the movement into an international story.
points: The Derry march of 5 October 1968 was organised by NICRA and was banned by the Minister of Home Affairs, William Craig.
Marchers who defied the ban were confronted by RUC officers, who used batons on the crowd in the Duke Street area.
Television footage of the violence was broadcast widely, and it shocked opinion in Britain and Ireland.
The event is seen as the start of the civil rights crisis of 1968 and 1969, as it moved the movement from marches to confrontation.
Nationalists in Derry saw the police action as proof of discrimination, while unionists blamed the civil rights organisers for provoking disorder.
The events in Derry led O'Neill to announce the reform programme, and they added urgency to the demands for an investigation.

notes.h: O'Neill's five-point reform package and the 'Crossroads' broadcast
notes.b: O'Neill's reform package was the government's response to the crisis, and it failed to end the protests because it came too late.
points: The five-point package, announced in late 1968, included one man, one vote in local government elections.
The package also promised a Commissioner for Complaints, an ombudsman to examine complaints against public bodies.
It proposed a Housing Executive to take control of public housing away from the councils.
It promised reform of the Londonderry Corporation, the body most criticised for gerrymandering in Derry.
O'Neill presented the package in the 'Ulster at the Crossroads' broadcast in December 1968, appealing to unionists to accept change.
Unionist hardliners opposed the package and some Stormont backbenchers rejected it, which weakened O'Neill's authority.

notes.h: People's Democracy, Burntollet and the O'Neill crisis, 1969
notes.b: The People's Democracy march to Derry was attacked at Burntollet, and the violence that followed brought O'Neill's government to its end.
points: People's Democracy was formed in October 1968 by students at Queen's University Belfast, including Bernadette Devlin.
The People's Democracy march from Belfast to Derry began on 1 January 1969, aiming to protest against discrimination and the police.
On 4 January 1969 the marchers were ambushed at Burntollet Bridge by loyalists, some of whom were off-duty B Specials.
The attack was followed by a clash between police and residents in the Bogside, which increased tension in Derry for days.
O'Neill's government was reluctant to act against the Burntollet attackers, which some unionists also regarded as a sign of weakness.
A Stormont general election was held on 24 February 1969, and O'Neill's supporters won a narrow majority, but his authority was badly weakened.
The Mid Ulster by-election of April 1969 returned Bernadette Devlin, which added to the pressure on O'Neill from his own supporters.
O'Neill resigned in April 1969 and was succeeded by James Chichester-Clark.

notes.b: Devlin was a student leader and civil rights activist who became the youngest woman elected to Westminster at the time.
points: Bernadette Devlin was born in 1947 in Cookstown, County Tyrone, and studied psychology at Queen's University Belfast.
She became a leader of People's Democracy and a prominent speaker in the civil rights campaign in 1968 and 1969.
She was elected MP for Mid Ulster at a by-election in April 1969, aged twenty-one, as a candidate of the civil rights movement.
She was a participant in the People's Democracy campaign that organised the Belfast to Derry march of January 1969.
She wrote a memoir, The Price of My Soul, published in 1969, which presented the civil rights struggle from her own perspective.
Contemporary nationalists saw her as a symbol of youth and defiance, while unionists regarded her as a dangerous agitator.
Historians tend to view her as a key figure who brought the civil rights movement into Westminster politics.

notes.b: Paisley's opposition to O'Neill made him the most visible unionist critic of reform before 1969.
points: Ian Paisley was born in 1926 in Armagh and founded the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster in 1951.
Before 1969 he was a minister and public campaigner, who organised rallies and protests against O'Neill's policies.
He opposed the Lemass meeting and argued that the Prime Minister was undermining Protestant identity and the Union.
He was a participant in the 'O'Neill must go' campaign, and his rallies mobilised grassroots Protestant opinion.
Contemporaries saw him as the voice of hardline unionism, and many moderate unionists were uneasy about his methods.
Historians argue that his campaign against O'Neill helped to shift unionist politics towards the hardline position of the 1970s.

notes.h: Assessment: O'Neill and the civil rights movement
points: Success: O'Neill's reforms, including the five-point package, conceded the main demands of the civil rights movement on local voting and housing.
Limit: the reforms came late, after the Derry march of October 1968, and many civil rights leaders judged them as concessions forced by protest.
Success: the movement put discrimination on the British political agenda and brought the question of Northern Ireland's government into the open.
Failure: O'Neill could not carry his party or the unionist community, and his resignation in April 1969 showed the limits of reform from above.
Contemporary view: nationalists welcomed the movement's gains but argued that the state had not yet ended discrimination.
Contemporary view: unionists were divided, with hardliners blaming the civil rights movement for provoking violence.
Later view: historians differ on whether O'Neill was a sincere reformer who was undermined, or a leader whose reforms were too limited and too late.
